newsitem.title: USA: Moody's ups State University System of Florida.
newsitem.headline: Moody's ups State University System of Florida.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service said it upgraded the debt rating of the State University System of Florida to Aa3 from Aa2, and assigned a stable outlook, in connection with an upcoming sale.

This upgrade primarily reflects the system's monopolistic market position in Florida, solid debt service coverage from mandatory student fees, balanced financial operations, and strong financial cushion.
The upgrade also applies to the underlying rating of the following University System Improvement Certificates:
-- Series 1991 (insured by AMBAC) in the outstanding amount of $45.1 million through 2016.
-- Series 1993 (insured by MBIA) in the outstanding amount of $87.0 million through 2013.

This upgrade primarily reflects the System's monopolistic market position in Florida, solid debt service coverage from mandatory student fees, balanced financial operations, and strong financial cushion.
The State University System of Florida is comprised of the state's nine public universities and enrolls almost 125,000 full-time-equivalent students.

The System is issuing $36.9 million of Series 1997 University System Improvement Bonds for public bid during the week of March 17 to fund a variety of capital projects. These bonds and parity certificates are backed by mandatory student fees assessed on all students of System universities.
The rating and outlook on the System Improvement Revenue are based on the following credit factors:

-- More than 200,000 total students are enrolled in the System, representing almost one third of all students attending two-year and four-year public or private institutions in Florida. The nine member universities, which include University of Florida and Florida State University, are located throughout the state, providing access to a significant number of transfers from Florida's large community college system as well as attracting 15% of all Florida high school graduates as freshmen.

-- Enrollment growth, averaging 5% annually, has allowed the System to maintain debt service coverage ranging from 1.3 to 2.1 times over the past five years--without raising the student building and capital improvement trust fund fees securing the bonds.

-- State appropriations comprise almost 50% of the System's aggregate revenue. State appropriations rose 7% from 1995 to 1996 despite a threatened reduction, continuing an improving trend following the 7% cut experienced during fiscal 1992.

-- The System enjoys a favorable financial cushion, reflected by its low aggregate debt and large foundation endowments. Direct debt of the System and its universities aggregates only $340 million after the current issue. Substantial resources are held for the benefit of member universities at affiliated foundations, aggregating over $1 billion.
